stories.headline: Delhi AQI crosses 400 after Deepavali as smog spreads to other cities
stories.summary: Delhi's air quality deteriorated sharply around Deepavali, with the city-wide AQI climbing past 400 and 15 monitoring locations entering the 'severe' band, while thick smog cut visibility across the capital. The Air Quality Early Warning System had forecast the slide into 'severe' from November 9 and expected it to persist for several days, with Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan already in force across Delhi-NCR. Firecracker use in defiance of the ban, combined with seasonal meteorological factors, drove the spike; parts of the city recorded particulate levels many times the WHO limit, and data were missing from several Delhi government monitoring stations during the worst hours. The episode was not confined to Delhi — Mumbai, Lucknow, Chennai and Hyderabad reported poor air, with Hyderabad's AQI averaging 509 and PM2.5 touching 392 micrograms per cubic metre at 9.30 p.m. Scroll.in reported that 98 of the world's 100 most polluted cities that day were in India, while Down To Earth placed the episode within a wider, year-round national crisis.
stories.whyItMatters: Air pollution is a recurring GS-III environment theme that also tests GS-II governance — CAQM/GRAP enforcement, municipal capacity and the public-health burden on the urban poor. Post-Deepavali episodes are a standard case study for evaluating emergency versus structural responses.

perspectives.take: Frames it as a national, multi-city event — Delhi at the edge of 'severe' with smog spreading to Mumbai, Lucknow and Chennai — and separately reports defiance of the cracker ban and missing data from government monitoring stations.

Rights-and-accountability lens, foregrounding the global comparison that 98 of the 100 most polluted cities that day were Indian.
Measured and data-led: notes Delhi's air stayed 'very poor' overall even as 15 locations recorded 'severe' AQI.
Critical, retrospective framing — 'most polluted Deepavali eve in a decade' — implying a decade-long policy failure rather than a one-night accident.
Long-run environmental-justice framing ('slow murder continues'), emphasising urban, rural and industrial exposure, health burden and setbacks from rising vehicle ownership and polluting fuels.

static.topic: Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) and Delhi-NCR air quality governance
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Ecology — Pollution and Environmental Governance
static.whatIsIt: GRAP is a graded, emergency-response framework of anti-pollution measures that kicks in across Delhi-NCR as the AQI worsens, moving from Stage I to Stage IV. It is invoked by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) in coordination with the NCR states.
static.background: GRAP was first notified in 2016 by the Supreme Court-appointed Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA), following directions in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India. The CAQM was created by an Ordinance in 2020 and given statutory backing by the CAQM Act, 2021, taking over EPCA's role for the NCR. The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), launched in 2019, targets reduction of PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations in identified non-attainment cities.
static.geography: Delhi-NCR spans Delhi and districts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan within the NCR Planning Board area; the Indo-Gangetic Plain's winter meteorology — low wind, temperature inversion and stubble-burning smoke — traps pollutants near the surface.
static.socioEconomic: Pollution episodes hit outdoor workers, street vendors, construction labour and schoolchildren hardest; health costs and lost workdays fall disproportionately on low-income households.
static.whyInNews: Post-Deepavali AQI in Delhi crossed 400 with Stage III of GRAP in force, and the Early Warning System forecast 'severe' conditions for the following days.
static.wayForward: Strengthen year-round source apportionment and monitoring, enforce cracker and stubble-burning bans credibly, expand public transport and clean-fuel transition, and give CAQM clear enforcement powers with state accountability.
prelimsPointers: GRAP is an emergency, graded action plan for Delhi-NCR invoked by CAQM; it is not a nationwide statutory standard.
NCAP (2019) targets reduction of PM2.5 and PM10 in non-attainment cities; CPCB is the apex pollution regulator under the Air Act, 1981.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether emergency, episodic measures like GRAP can substitute for structural, year-round action on vehicular, industrial, dust and biomass sources of air pollution.

static.topic: Urban local governance and municipal capacity in pollution control
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Local Self-Government (74th Amendment)
static.whatIsIt: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to panchayats and municipalities, mandating regular elections, reservations and State Finance Commissions. The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 municipal functions, including public health, sanitation, solid waste management and urban planning — the levers most relevant to local air quality.
static.background: Lord Ripon's Resolution of 1882 is treated as the foundation of local self-government in India. The Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules list 29 and 18 subjects respectively. Urban missions such as the Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, Swachh Bharat and PMAY operate through municipal bodies.
static.socioEconomic: Weak own-source revenue and dependence on transfers limit municipal capacity; pollution control competes with water, waste and transport for the same thin budgets.
static.whyInNews: Delhi and other cities recorded severe AQI after Deepavali, renewing scrutiny of how municipal bodies enforce bans on firecrackers, construction dust and waste burning.
static.wayForward: Deepen fiscal devolution through State Finance Commissions, build technical capacity in urban local bodies, and integrate air-quality action plans into city master plans and budgets.
keyTerms: Nagar Panchayat / Municipal Council / Municipal Corporation
prelimsPointers: Three types of municipalities: Nagar Panchayat (transitional), Municipal Council (smaller urban area), Municipal Corporation (larger urban area).
The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 municipal subjects; the Eleventh Schedule lists 29 panchayat subjects.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how weak fiscal devolution and capacity gaps in urban local bodies undermine enforcement of environmental and public-health regulations in Indian cities.

static.topic: Health burden of air pollution and the welfare response
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare, Rights and Health
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare model blends rights-based laws (MGNREGA 2005, RTE 2009, NFSA 2013) with DBT-enabled schemes and a JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) delivery backbone. Ayushman Bharat (2018) has a health-insurance arm (PM-JAY) and Health & Wellness Centres.
static.background: POSHAN Abhiyaan targets malnutrition; Article 15/16 and Indra Sawhney (1992) frame reservation policy. Air pollution adds a chronic disease burden — respiratory and cardiovascular illness — that intersects with undernutrition and out-of-pocket health spending.
static.socioEconomic: Reduced life expectancy and millions of premature deaths are linked to foul air; the burden falls hardest on outdoor workers, the poor and children, who cannot buy protection.
static.whyInNews: Post-Deepavali smog across Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad and other cities has renewed attention to the health costs of air pollution.
static.wayForward: Integrate air-quality advisories with primary health surveillance, expand PM-JAY coverage for pollution-linked respiratory illness, and target vulnerable occupational groups.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 labour laws.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how environmental health risks interact with welfare exclusion and capability deprivation among India's urban poor.

prelims: India's AQI categories: Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderate (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400) and Severe (401–500).
GRAP is a graded emergency action plan for Delhi-NCR invoked by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), set up in 2020 and given statutory backing by the CAQM Act, 2021.
PM2.5 — fine particulate matter under 2.5 micrometres — is the key health-damaging pollutant; the WHO's 2021 guideline is an annual mean of 5 micrograms per cubic metre.
The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 are the principal statutes; the CPCB is the apex pollution regulator.
stories.mainsQuestion: Emergency measures such as the Graded Response Action Plan have not prevented recurring post-Deepavali air quality emergencies in Delhi-NCR. Examine why episodic, city-centric interventions fail, and suggest a structural, multi-sectoral framework for clean air in India.

stories.headline: COP31 opens in Antalya as climate targets face delivery test
stories.summary: COP31 opened in Antalya, Türkiye, with more than 100,000 participants expected over two weeks, as climate and geopolitical pressures mount. The summit is taking place amid a widening gap between countries' climate pledges and actual implementation, with calls for measurable progress rather than more deals. On the sidelines, the IEA chief cited India's renewable energy expansion as a lesson for emerging economies facing global uncertainty. A separate editorial drew attention to the hidden toll of climate change on reproductive health, adding a public-health and social-justice dimension to the climate debate.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the credibility of the Paris Agreement's ratchet mechanism, NDC implementation, climate finance and India's renewable-energy diplomacy; also links climate governance with health and welfare outcomes.

perspectives.take: Frames COP31 as a high-attendance summit unfolding under simultaneous climate and geopolitical pressures, emphasising scale and stakes.
Argues that new climate deals are insufficient unless countries deliver measurable results, closing the target-implementation gap.

static.topic: Climate Change Regime & India's Commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change
static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle. Paris uses NDCs and a ratchet mechanism. Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and LiFE mission.
static.socioEconomic: Climate finance and technology transfer gaps shape developing-country implementation; just transition concerns affect workers and vulnerable communities.
static.whyInNews: COP31 in Antalya is assessing delivery of climate targets; the IEA chief cited India's renewable expansion as a lesson for emerging economies.
static.wayForward: Strengthen measurable implementation, scale climate finance and technology transfer, and integrate equity and just transition into NDC updates and Global Stocktake follow-up.

static.topic: United Nations & Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.socioEconomic: Multilateral legitimacy and decision-making affect global climate, development and security cooperation, including implementation of UNFCCC commitments.
static.whyInNews: COP31 highlights the role of UN-led climate multilateralism amid geopolitical pressures and demands for effective delivery.
static.wayForward: Revitalise multilateral institutions and make climate governance more representative, transparent and implementation-focused.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN HQ is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim rests on representativeness, its population and contributions; assess obstacles (veto politics, Africa's Ezulwini Consensus).

stories.headline: G7 meets in Paris as Iran diplomacy stalls; Iraq's Khor Mor gas field hit
stories.summary: Diplomatic efforts around the US–Iran conflict stalled as G7 foreign ministers gathered in Paris, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying Washington preferred a negotiated solution but describing Tehran's demands as "outrageous and ridiculous". President Trump is due to meet Qatar's prime minister at the White House to discuss Doha's mediation efforts, even as he called fresh strikes on Iran "unlikely" — a remark that pushed oil prices lower. Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said the "mission is not complete" on Iran, alleging Tehran is renewing efforts to obtain nuclear weapons. Separately, production was suspended at Iraq's Khor Mor gas field after a drone attack hit a gas storage facility, with crew ordered into shelters amid fear of further strikes. Rubio defended the more than eight-month-old war even as voters blamed Trump's policies for higher energy prices stemming from disruptions to shipments in the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.whyItMatters: West Asia remains the pivot of India's energy security, diaspora welfare and balancing diplomacy; the trajectory of the US–Iran conflict, G7 coordination and Gulf mediation directly shapes India's crude import bill, inflation and strategic autonomy choices.

static.topic: India's Foreign Policy & Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks. It engages across the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA simultaneously.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and Quad (with US, Japan, Australia) gained salience after 2017.
static.geography: West Asia and the Persian Gulf form India's extended neighbourhood — a source of crude and LNG, a host to a large Indian diaspora, and a theatre where India balances ties with the US, Israel, Gulf states and Iran.
static.socioEconomic: Higher energy prices and shipping disruptions in the Gulf transmit into India's import bill, current account and inflation; Gulf remittances support household incomes and state economies.
static.whyInNews: The stalled US–Iran diplomacy, the Paris G7 ministerial, Qatar's mediation role and Israel's stated position all test India's balancing act between Washington, Tehran and the Gulf.
static.wayForward: Sustain multi-alignment, diversify crude and LNG sourcing, protect diaspora interests, back de-escalation and regional mediation, and keep independent channels open with all parties.
prelimsPointers: India assumed the G20 presidency in 2022–23; the African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023.
India and Pakistan joined the SCO in 2017.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing ties with the West, Russia and the Global South; India as a 'Voice of the Global South' and bridging power — assess in the context of a West Asia conflict.

static.wayForward: Press for UNSC expansion through the G4 and IGN while using plurilateral and minilateral formats as complements, not substitutes, for UN-centred multilateralism.

static.topic: Strait of Hormuz & Energy Security
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Energy Security
static.whatIsIt: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway linking the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, and is a critical chokepoint for seaborne crude oil and LNG shipments.
static.background: It has been a recurring flashpoint in US–Iran tensions, with Iran repeatedly threatening closure during past standoffs and periodic tanker seizures and attacks in the Gulf of Oman and Hormuz approaches.
static.geography: It lies between Iran to the north and Oman and the UAE to the south; the navigable shipping lanes pass through Iranian and Omani territorial waters.
static.socioEconomic: Any disruption raises crude prices, freight and insurance costs, feeding imported inflation in India and tightening LNG availability for industry and utilities.
static.whyInNews: Rubio attributed higher energy prices to disruptions to shipments in the Strait of Hormuz during the US–Iran war, while oil prices fell after Trump said new attacks were 'unlikely'.
static.wayForward: Diversify crude sourcing, expand and use strategic petroleum reserves, deepen cooperation with producer and consumer forums, and accelerate renewables and electrification to blunt chokepoint risk.
prelimsPointers: A large share of the world's seaborne crude oil and LNG passes through the Strait of Hormuz.
India's strategic petroleum reserves are located at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
static.mainsAngle: Chokepoint geopolitics and India's energy security — examine diversification, strategic reserves and the shift to renewables as buffers against supply shocks.

prelims: The G7 comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States; its foreign ministers met in Paris.

stories.mainsQuestion: The US–Iran conflict and the resulting chokepoint risks in the Strait of Hormuz have direct consequences for India's energy security and diplomatic balancing. Examine how India can reconcile its strategic autonomy with its energy and diaspora interests in West Asia.

stories.summary: CERT-In has flagged an AI-driven hacking campaign named 'Crafty Falcon' that targets Indian fintech firms, according to The Indian Express. The alert focuses attention on the cyber-security vulnerabilities of a sector that handles large volumes of digital financial transactions. It also highlights the expanding threat surface created by India's digital public infrastructure and rapid fintech adoption. CERT-In, as the national nodal agency for cyber-incident response, is central to detecting and advising on such campaigns. The report does not, in the supplied material, detail the campaign's methods or the number of firms affected.

static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure — Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker — is a layered, interoperable stack. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data processing.
static.background: Aadhaar (UIDAI, 2009) is the world's largest biometric ID. UPI (NPCI, 2016) processes billions of monthly transactions. The DPDP Act introduces a Data Protection Board and consent-based processing.
static.geography: India
static.socioEconomic: DPI supports financial inclusion and digital payments; cyber attacks on fintech can undermine trust and inclusion gains.
static.whyInNews: The CERT-In alert on AI-driven hacking of fintech firms highlights security risks to India's digital financial ecosystem.
static.wayForward: Enforce DPDP compliance, strengthen CERT-In advisories, promote public-private threat intelligence, and build cyber resilience in DPI-linked services.

Simultaneously, loyalists within his MAGA base have begun openly questioning his role in the Republican defeats, while Trump and his Justice Department have taken a defiant posture towards the investigative agenda Democrats are preparing, with Trump describing their requests as 'extortion at the highest level'. static.topic: US Midterm Elections and the American Political Cycle
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: Midterm elections are held midway through a US President's four-year term, when all 435 seats of the House of Representatives, roughly one-third of the 100-member Senate, and a large number of state governorships and legislatures go to the polls.
static.background: The US Constitution (Article I) fixes two-year terms for the House and six-year staggered terms for the Senate, so elections necessarily fall in every even-numbered year. A recurring pattern — the 'president's party penalty' — is that the incumbent president's party loses seats in the midterms, often producing divided government and a hostile or partially hostile Congress for the remaining two years.
static.geography: United States — a federal union of 50 states; elections are administered by state and county authorities under a decentralised system.
static.socioEconomic: Midterm verdicts typically turn on cost of living, inflation, jobs and immigration; enforcement crackdowns can tighten labour supply in agriculture, construction, hospitality and services, and unsettle migrant and diaspora communities.
static.whyInNews: Trump's post-midterm admission that his deportation policy was 'too tough', internal MAGA criticism of his role in Republican losses, and the Democratic investigative push in the new Congress.
static.wayForward: For India, the practical watch-list is visa and mobility policy (H-1B, student visas, green-card backlogs), tariff and trade posture, and diaspora safety; for Washington, divided government usually means legislative gridlock combined with intensified oversight.
prelimsPointers: US House of Representatives: 435 voting members, two-year terms; Senate: 100 members, six-year staggered terms.
The US President is elected indirectly through the Electoral College for a four-year term, limited to two terms by the 22nd Amendment.
Midterm elections are held in November of even-numbered years, i.e. midway through the presidential term.
static.mainsAngle: How do midterm reversals in the United States reshape the president's domestic and foreign policy room, and what should India watch for?

static.topic: US Immigration and Deportation Regime
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies of developed countries on India's interests; Indian diaspora
static.whatIsIt: US immigration law governs admission, status and removal of foreign nationals. The Immigration and Nationality Act (1952, repeatedly amended) is the core statute; enforcement is split between the Department of Homeland Security (ICE, CBP, USCIS) and the Department of Justice's immigration courts.
static.background: The 1952 McCarran-Walter Act consolidated earlier immigration statutes; the 1965 Hart-Celler Act abolished national-origins quotas and shifted to a family- and skills-based system; the 1986 IRCA legalised a section of undocumented workers; the 1996 IIRIRA expanded grounds for removal and expedited removal; the H-1B non-immigrant work visa was created by the Immigration Act of 1990. Comprehensive reform bills have repeatedly stalled in Congress, so policy has swung largely through executive action.
static.geography: The US–Mexico land border, roughly 3,100 km long, is the principal corridor for irregular migration into the United States.
static.socioEconomic: Undocumented workers are concentrated in agriculture, construction, food processing and hospitality; remittances are a lifeline for Mexico and Central America. Indian nationals are a major cohort in legal migration — students, H-1B workers and their dependants — and face long employment-based green-card queues.
static.whyInNews: Trump's post-midterm remark that his deportation policy was 'too tough' and that it hurt him electorally, signalling a possible softening in tone on enforcement.
static.wayForward: Given persistent congressional deadlock, predictability for Indian skilled migrants depends on administrative rules and litigation rather than legislation; India's engagement should track visa processing, per-country caps and consular capacity.
prelimsPointers: H-1B is a non-immigrant (temporary) work visa for specialty occupations, sponsored by a US employer.
Employment-based immigrant visas are subject to a per-country limit of 7 per cent of the annual total, which creates long backlogs for Indian applicants.
Birthright citizenship in the US flows from the Citizenship Clause of the 14th Amendment (1868).
static.mainsAngle: Examine how shifts in US immigration enforcement affect India's skilled-migration interests and the wider Indian diaspora.

static.topic: Separation of Powers and Congressional Oversight in the United States
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Comparison of the Indian constitutional scheme with that of other countries
static.whatIsIt: The US Constitution (1787, in force 1789) distributes power among the legislature, executive and judiciary with an elaborate system of checks and balances. Congress oversees the executive through committee hearings, subpoenas, contempt proceedings and, ultimately, impeachment.
static.background: Article I vests legislative power in Congress; its committees possess subpoena power, and refusal to comply can lead to a contempt of Congress citation, pursued criminally through the Justice Department or civilly in court. Impeachment is initiated in the House and tried in the Senate, where a two-thirds majority is needed for conviction. The Watergate hearings (1973–74) and the two presidential impeachments of 2019 and 2021 are the standard precedents.
static.whyInNews: Democrats are preparing an investigative blitz in the new Congress, while Trump has called their requests 'extortion at the highest level' and his Justice Department has signalled defiance.
static.wayForward: Divided government typically yields legislative gridlock plus aggressive oversight; watch for subpoena litigation, executive-privilege claims and how much executive bandwidth is consumed by domestic investigations at the cost of foreign policy attention.
prelimsPointers: The US Vice-President is ex-officio President of the Senate and may cast a tie-breaking vote.
Ratification of treaties requires a two-thirds majority in the US Senate; the House plays no role in treaty ratification.
The US Constitution is the oldest written national constitution still in force.
static.mainsAngle: Compare the US system of congressional oversight with India's parliamentary committee system and motions of no confidence.

static.topic: Semiconductor Supply Chains and US–China Technology Rivalry
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Semiconductors, Industrial Policy and Supply-Chain Security
static.whatIsIt: Semiconductors are the foundational input for computing, AI, defence and communications. Design (Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm), fabrication (TSMC, Samsung, Intel) and assembly-testing (ATMP/OSAT) are geographically concentrated, making chips a strategic asset and a target of export controls.
static.background: US export controls since 2022 progressively restricted advanced chipmaking tools and AI accelerators to China, and Nvidia developed China-market variants within those limits. India launched the India Semiconductor Mission in December 2021 with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore, and has since approved fab, ATMP and compound-semiconductor units, including in Gujarat and Assam.
static.geography: Fabrication is concentrated in Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, the US and mainland China; India's emerging clusters include Dholera and Sanand in Gujarat and Jagiroad in Assam.
static.socioEconomic: Chip shortages affect autos, electronics and defence; semiconductor investment is a major employment and export opportunity for India, but the sector is capital- and skill-intensive.
static.whyInNews: A board-level investigation at Nvidia, the dominant AI chip designer, has renewed attention on how far national-security concerns now shape the semiconductor industry and its China exposure.
static.wayForward: Diversify supply chains through trusted-partner arrangements, deepen India's design and ATMP ecosystem under the India Semiconductor Mission, and build critical-mineral and talent pipelines while keeping export-control compliance auditable.
prelimsPointers: The India Semiconductor Mission was launched in December 2021 with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore.

static.topic: Economic Espionage and Counter-Intelligence in the Technology Sector
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — State-Sponsored Espionage and Protection of Critical Technologies
static.whatIsIt: Economic espionage is the state-sponsored acquisition of trade secrets, proprietary technology and strategic information from private firms. It targets corporate leadership, researchers, diaspora networks and joint ventures, blurring the line between commercial competition and national security.
static.background: Counter-intelligence agencies such as the FBI in the US and the Intelligence Bureau and R&AW in India handle espionage threats. The PRC's National Intelligence Law (2017) obliges organisations and individuals to assist state intelligence work, which has sharpened scrutiny of Chinese-linked commercial and academic engagements in Western countries.
static.socioEconomic: Screening of collaborations can chill legitimate research and diaspora ties, so states balance openness against security vetting; firms face reputational and market-access costs.
static.whyInNews: Reports that Nvidia is investigating whether its CEO was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort have put corporate counter-intelligence and executive vulnerability in focus.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise insider-threat and counter-intelligence protocols in strategic firms, strengthen research-security guidelines in universities, and pursue reciprocal legal frameworks rather than blanket exclusion.
prelimsPointers: The PRC's National Intelligence Law of 2017 requires organisations and citizens to assist state intelligence work.
In India, the Intelligence Bureau handles internal counter-intelligence while R&AW focuses on external intelligence.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how economic espionage has become an instrument of strategic competition and suggest a calibrated framework for India to protect critical technologies without discouraging legitimate foreign collaboration.

static.topic: Corporate Governance, Key-Man Risk and Leadership Succession
static.syllabusNode: Corporate Governance — Board Oversight, Disclosure and Succession Planning
static.whatIsIt: Corporate governance concerns the systems by which companies are directed and controlled: independent board oversight, disclosure of material events, and succession planning. 'Key-man risk' is the concentration of a firm's strategic value in a single leader.
static.background: India's Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI's LODR Regulations require independent directors, audit committees and timely disclosure of material information; the Kotak Committee (2017) strengthened board independence and disclosure norms for listed companies.
static.socioEconomic: Weak succession planning and governance failures destroy shareholder value and can affect index-level market stability, especially in globally significant technology firms.
static.whyInNews: Nvidia's board launched an internal investigation after its CEO acknowledged a relationship that US intelligence linked to information-gathering for Beijing, raising questions about governance, disclosure and succession at a systemically important firm.
static.wayForward: Strengthen board-led succession pipelines, mandate prompt disclosure of material risks including security-related ones, and separate oversight of CEO conduct from day-to-day management.
prelimsPointers: The Companies Act, 2013 mandates independent directors and audit committees for prescribed classes of companies.
SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 govern disclosure and governance norms for listed entities.
static.mainsAngle: Corporate governance is no longer only about shareholder value; it is also about national-security and systemic-risk management. Critically examine.

stories.headline: Eisenkot mandated to form Israeli government, seeks wide coalition
stories.summary: Gadi Eisenkot, 66, a former IDF chief who entered electoral politics in 2022, formally received the presidential mandate on 8 November 2026 to form Israel's next government, even though his bloc lacks a clear Knesset majority. Warning that the country faces a deep crisis, he said he would seek a 'wide' government and publicly invited Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party to join a coalition under his leadership, saying it would be welcome. Under Israeli law the Prime Minister-designate initially has 28 days, extendable by 14, to assemble the confidence of at least 61 members in the 120-seat Knesset. The path to power remains uncertain, with coalition arithmetic and the posture of rival blocs still unsettled.
stories.whyItMatters: A change of guard in Israel bears directly on the Gaza conflict, ceasefire and normalisation diplomacy, and hence on India's energy, diaspora and defence interests in West Asia — a recurring GS-II International Relations theme. It also tests how far a broad, cross-bloc coalition can restore political stability in a deeply polarised polity.

static.whatIsIt: Israel has a parliamentary system with a 120-member Knesset elected by proportional representation. static.whyInNews: A possible change of government in Israel raises questions about continuity in defence contracts, technology cooperation and India's broader West Asia outreach.

stories.headline: Hasina seeks new passport as Dhaka presses India for extradition
stories.summary: Bangladesh's ousted former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has applied for a fresh passport and national identity card, a move read as the clearest signal yet that she intends to return home from exile in India. Dhaka says it has formally sought her extradition under the bilateral treaty, citing her conviction and death sentence handed down by the country's International Crimes Tribunal for crimes against humanity. Hasina has been in India since she left Dhaka in August 2024 amid mass protests against her government. New Delhi has so far not acted on the request, and the case has become the sharpest irritant in an otherwise deep, multi-stranded relationship. The passport question matters because a valid travel document is a precondition for any return, whether voluntary or court-ordered.

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Extradition Treaty and the Extradition Act, 1962
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral agreements and legal cooperation with neighbours
static.whatIsIt: A bilateral treaty between India and Bangladesh governing the mutual surrender of persons accused or convicted of offences, operating alongside India's domestic Extradition Act, 1962, which sets out the procedure and the grounds on which a request may be refused.
static.background: India's Extradition Act, 1962 consolidated the law on the subject and empowers the Central Government to notify treaty partners and to issue requests through magistrates. The India–Bangladesh extradition treaty was signed in 2013 and amended in 2016 to tighten provisions, including on fugitives claiming political motives. Requests under such treaties are examined judicially in the requested state, and refusal is permissible where the offence is regarded as political in character or where fair-trial safeguards are not met.
static.geography: A long, porous land border of over 4,000 km, with shared river systems and enclaves, makes cross-border movement and policing a structural feature of the relationship.
static.socioEconomic: Deep people-to-people, trade and transit linkages mean legal disputes between the two states carry direct economic and social costs for border communities and traders.
static.whyInNews: Bangladesh has said it formally sought Hasina's extradition from India after her conviction and death sentence, while she has applied for a new passport — both steps that engage the treaty framework.
static.wayForward: India should articulate a transparent, law-based position on the request, allowing judicial processes under the Extradition Act to run while insulating the wider relationship from a single case.
prelimsPointers: India's Extradition Act was enacted in 1962 and governs both treaty-based and non-treaty extradition requests.
The India–Bangladesh extradition treaty was signed in 2013 and amended in 2016.

static.mainsAngle: Examine how extradition treaties balance sovereign discretion with international legal obligation, using India's neighbourhood as a case study.

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Relations and the 'Neighbourhood First' Approach
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The bilateral relationship spanning trade, connectivity, energy, water-sharing, security cooperation and people-to-people ties, anchored for India in its Neighbourhood First policy.
static.background: Bangladesh was carved out of Pakistan in 1971 with decisive Indian military and diplomatic support. Ties improved markedly after 2009 through land boundary settlement (2015), the Ganga water-sharing treaty (1996), power-grid interconnection, and cooperation on transit and connectivity. Political transitions in Dhaka have repeatedly tested the relationship, since India's stakes are with whichever government holds office.
static.geography: Bangladesh surrounds India on the east and shares borders with West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; it is India's largest trading partner in South Asia and a critical transit corridor to the Northeast.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is among India's largest export markets in the region; connectivity projects, power supply and port access generate substantial mutual economic gains, while migration and border management remain sensitive.
static.whyInNews: The extradition demand and Hasina's continued presence in India have become the dominant irritant in ties, testing India's ability to separate a legal dispute from strategic partnership.
static.wayForward: India should maintain principled, quiet diplomacy, protect ongoing connectivity and trade gains, and engage the current Bangladeshi government on security and economic agendas irrespective of the outcome of the Hasina case.
prelimsPointers: The India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement was operationalised in 2015, exchanging enclaves.
The Ganga Water Sharing Treaty between India and Bangladesh dates to 1996.
Bangladesh is a key partner in BBIN (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal) sub-regional connectivity.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how political instability in a neighbouring state affects India's Neighbourhood First policy, and suggest how India can de-risk bilateral ties.

static.topic: Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal and Transitional Justice
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Comparative politics and governance; human rights
static.whatIsIt: A domestic tribunal established by Bangladesh in 2010 to try crimes against humanity, genocide and war crimes connected to the 1971 liberation war and, in later practice, other grave offences.
static.background: The tribunal was set up under the International Crimes (Tribunals) Act, 1973, revived in 2010. It has delivered judgments against several political figures, drawing criticism from international observers over due-process standards while enjoying broad domestic political support. Appeals lie to Bangladesh's Appellate Division.
static.socioEconomic: Verdicts are politically charged in a country where the 1971 war remains a foundational identity question, and they shape party politics and street mobilisation.
static.whyInNews: Hasina's conviction and death sentence by the tribunal is the legal basis cited by Dhaka for its extradition request to India.
static.wayForward: India should track the appellate process and due-process questions carefully, since the credibility of the underlying proceedings will shape any eventual legal or diplomatic response.
prelimsPointers: Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal was established in 2010 under a 1973 law.
The tribunal tries crimes against humanity, genocide and war crimes linked to the 1971 conflict.
Appeals against tribunal verdicts go to the Appellate Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the tension between domestic transitional-justice mechanisms and international due-process standards in post-conflict societies.

This is described as a record period without prorogation. Because the session has not been ended, the government retains the option of convening an extended sitting of the same session rather than summoning a fresh one. The development turns attention to parliamentary procedure, session management and the constitutional distinction between adjournment, prorogation and dissolution.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests understanding of parliamentary sessions, Article 85, prorogation versus adjournment and dissolution, and how session continuity affects pending Bills, ordinances and executive accountability.

static.topic: Prorogation of Parliament and Session Continuity
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Prorogation is the formal termination of a session of Parliament by the President, on the advice of the Council of Ministers, under Article 85. It differs from adjournment, which only suspends a sitting, and from dissolution, which ends the Lok Sabha's life.
static.background: The Constitution of India provides for summoning and prorogation of the Houses under Article 85. A session runs from summoning to prorogation; adjournment is ordered by the presiding officer and does not end the session. Pending Bills do not lapse merely on prorogation; dissolution of the Lok Sabha has specific consequences for pending legislation. Ordinances under Article 123 can be promulgated when Parliament is not in session and must be approved within six weeks of reassembly.
static.socioEconomic: Prolonged unprorogued sessions can affect legislative planning, budget timelines, ordinance promulgation and accountability to elected representatives.
static.whyInNews: As of November 9, 2026, the Monsoon session had not been prorogued for 88 days, a record, keeping the existing session available for an extended sitting.
static.wayForward: Session calendars should be predictable; legislative business should be routed through committees; prolonged unprorogued periods should not become a substitute for regular sittings or normal legislative scrutiny.
prelimsPointers: Prorogation ends a session; adjournment only postpones a sitting within the same session.
A Bill pending in Parliament does not lapse merely because of prorogation; dissolution of the Lok Sabha has specific consequences.
An Ordinance must be approved by Parliament within six weeks of its reassembly.
Under Article 85, the President summons and prorogues the Houses on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how prolonged non-prorogation and irregular parliamentary sittings affect legislative scrutiny, executive accountability and the use of the ordinance route.

stories.mainsQuestion: The Constitution allows Parliament to remain unprorogued, but prolonged non-prorogation raises questions of legislative accountability. Examine the procedural and constitutional implications, and suggest safeguards for regular parliamentary scrutiny.

static.topic: Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Energy, Infrastructure and Biofuels
static.whatIsIt: A programme under which ethanol — produced from sugarcane juice, molasses, sugar syrup, maize, damaged food grains and surplus rice — is blended with petrol by oil marketing companies (OMCs) to cut crude import dependence and vehicular emissions. Ethanol is procured by OMCs through tenders at administered prices for different feedstock categories.
static.background: The EBP programme began in 2003. The National Policy on Biofuels, 2018 (amended 2022) provided the policy architecture and feedstock expansion, including advanced biofuels and surplus grain diversion. The 20% blending (E20) target was advanced from 2030 to 2025, prompting expansion of distillery capacity, E20-compatible vehicles and flex-fuel technology. Blending percentages rose sharply over the past decade from low single digits.
static.geography: Ethanol supply is concentrated in sugarcane-growing states — Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka — along with grain-based distilleries in maize belts; distribution logistics to deficit states remain a constraint.
static.socioEconomic: Blending supports sugar mill viability and cane payment cycles, creates demand for maize, and reduces the oil import bill, but raises questions on diversion of food grains, competition with feed and poultry demand, and the high water intensity of sugarcane.
static.whyInNews: Karnataka conducted petrol sample testing at 67 locations following complaints about ethanol-blended fuel quality, covering blending and distribution stages as well as retail pumps.
static.wayForward: Strengthen testing infrastructure and certification at blending depots, rationalise feedstock pricing, diversify to second-generation and non-food feedstock, and monitor food-security and water trade-offs.
prelimsPointers: EBP is administered by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas; OMCs procure ethanol through tenders.
The E20 target was advanced from 2030 to 2025 under the amended Biofuels policy framework.
Ethanol feedstock includes sugarcane juice, B- and C-heavy molasses, sugar syrup, maize, damaged food grains and surplus rice.
static.mainsAngle: Rapid scaling of ethanol blending versus food security, water use and fuel quality — how should India sequence its energy transition in transport fuels?

static.topic: MSP, Sugarcane Pricing and Food Security
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Agriculture and Food Security
static.whatIsIt: Minimum Support Price (MSP) is announced by the government on CACP recommendations for 22 mandated crops. Food security is backed by the National Food Security Act, 2013, and the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana grain distribution. Sugarcane additionally has a Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) fixed by the Centre, with states often announcing a higher State Advised Price.
static.background: The Green Revolution (1960s) made India food-sufficient. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) reviewed FCI operations. PM-KISAN gives ₹6,000 a year as income support. The three 2020 farm laws were repealed in 2021.
static.geography: Cane cultivation is concentrated in irrigated tracts of Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka; procurement of wheat and paddy is similarly concentrated in a few states.
static.socioEconomic: MSP is a price assurance, not a legal right, and procurement is skewed towards wheat and paddy. Ethanol demand adds a new purchaser for sugarcane and maize, but can affect cane arrears, cropping patterns and grain availability.
static.whyInNews: Ethanol-blended fuel quality complaints in Karnataka link the blending programme back to sugarcane and grain economics — the same agrarian value chain that MSP and FRP policies govern.
static.wayForward: Reform MSP and procurement while raising farmer incomes; balance ethanol diversion with food security and water-fertiliser sustainability.
prelimsPointers: MSP is a price assurance, not a legal right; procurement is concentrated in wheat and paddy.
NFSA covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.

static.mainsAngle: Reforming MSP and procurement while raising farmer incomes; aligning ethanol feedstock demand with sustainable cropping patterns.

static.topic: Petrol and Diesel Pricing in India

static.whatIsIt: Retail petrol and diesel prices are market-determined, set by the oil marketing companies (IOCL, BPCL, HPCL) as the sum of the base price, central excise duty, dealer commission and state VAT.
static.background: The Administered Pricing Mechanism for petroleum products was dismantled in 2002. Petrol was deregulated in 2010 and diesel in 2014. Daily price revision was introduced in June 2017. OMCs have also kept retail prices unchanged for extended periods in recent years.
static.geography: Prices vary across cities mainly because of differing state VAT rates and freight; Delhi typically has one of the lower metro retail rates.
static.socioEconomic: Fuel prices feed into transport costs and inflation and have a regressive incidence, while excise duty and VAT are a major revenue source for the Centre and states.
static.whyInNews: Reported retail rates of ₹102.12 a litre for petrol and ₹95.20 for diesel in Delhi, with the national capital among the cheaper metros.
static.wayForward: Consider bringing petroleum products under GST to reduce cascading and rate disparities, while addressing revenue implications for both tiers of government.
prelimsPointers: Petrol and diesel remain outside the GST net and attract central excise duty plus state VAT.
Daily price revision based on international benchmarks began in June 2017.
Petrol was deregulated in 2010 and diesel in 2014, ending administered pricing.

stories.headline: UK High Court hears Hindu family's tilak discrimination case against London school
stories.summary: The parents of a nine-year-old Hindu boy have moved the UK High Court alleging religious discrimination after a London school prevented their son from wearing the tilak-chandlo on its premises. Reports dated 8 November 2026 indicate the family argues that the forehead mark is an integral part of their religious practice rather than a discretionary ornament, and that the school's objection amounts to a denial of the right to manifest belief. The school's position, as reflected in the coverage, rests on its uniform and neutrality rules. The case is being tracked in the Indian press as part of a wider pattern of disputes over religious symbols in secular public institutions. It raises questions about how far institutional dress codes must go in accommodating religious practice.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live example of the tension between institutional neutrality and the right to manifest religion — directly relevant to Articles 25–28, the essential religious practices test, and comparative secularism questions in GS-I and GS-II. It also supplies a contemporary illustration for essays on multiculturalism and reasonable accommodation.

static.topic: Freedom of Religion (Articles 25–28)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Fundamental Rights
static.whatIsIt: Articles 25–28 guarantee freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion (Art. 25), rights of religious denominations to manage their own affairs (Art. 26), freedom from taxation for the promotion of any religion (Art. 27) and restrictions on religious instruction in state-funded institutions (Art. 28).
static.background: Shaped by Constituent Assembly debates on secularism. The 'essential religious practices' test traces to Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmi Shirur Mutt (1954). Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) protected the right of Jehovah's Witnesses students not to sing the national anthem; the Sabarimala judgment (2018) applied the test to temple-entry restrictions. State-mandated dress codes have repeatedly been tested against Article 25.
static.socioEconomic: India's religious pluralism means accommodation disputes arise in schools, workplaces and public institutions, with costs falling unevenly on minorities and on students.
static.whyInNews: A UK court is hearing a parallel dispute over a Hindu pupil's tilak, inviting comparison with Indian jurisprudence on religious symbols.
static.wayForward: Prefer reasonable accommodation through institutional rules, guidelines and dialogue over adversarial litigation; evolve clear, religion-neutral criteria that respect genuine religious mandates.
prelimsPointers: Article 25 is available to all persons, including non-citizens; Article 26 is available only to religious denominations.
Article 28(1) bars religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of state funds.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether the 'essential religious practices' doctrine is an adequate tool for resolving modern disputes over religious symbols in public institutions.

static.topic: Judicial Review and Constitutional Courts
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Art. 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Art. 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power of courts to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution. The UK High Court performs an analogous supervisory function under its own constitutional arrangements.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Writs under Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) are the principal remedies.
static.socioEconomic: Judicial remedies are the practical route for minorities and individuals contesting institutional decisions, but cost, delay and pendency constrain access.
static.whyInNews: The tilak dispute has been taken to the UK High Court, illustrating constitutional courts as fora for rights claims against institutional rules.
static.wayForward: Strengthen access to justice through legal aid, alternative dispute resolution and reduced pendency, while preserving judicial independence.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction over Centre–state disputes lies with the Supreme Court under Article 131.
Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is under Article 143.
static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial backlog, vacancies and pendency; the balance between judicial independence and accountability.

static.topic: Multiculturalism and Reasonable Accommodation
static.syllabusNode: Society — Diversity, Pluralism and Multiculturalism
static.whatIsIt: Multiculturalism refers to State policies and social arrangements that recognise and accommodate distinct cultural and religious identities within a shared public framework, rather than requiring assimilation into a single dominant norm.
static.background: In the UK, anti-discrimination law evolved from the Race Relations Acts (1965, 1968, 1976) and related statutes, consolidated in the Equality Act 2010, which lists religion or belief among nine protected characteristics. The Human Rights Act 1998 gives domestic effect to the European Convention on Human Rights, whose Article 9 protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including manifestation subject to limitations prescribed by law. European debates over religious symbols in schools and workplaces have produced divergent national outcomes.
static.socioEconomic: Accommodation disputes typically pit institutional uniformity and administrative convenience against the practical cost borne by minority pupils and employees.
static.whyInNews: The London school tilak case is the latest instance of a religious-symbol dispute being adjudicated under anti-discrimination and human-rights law.
static.wayForward: Adopt published accommodation policies, engage affected communities early, and use proportionality-based tests that weigh institutional aims against the burden on the individual.
prelimsPointers: The UK Equality Act 2010 consolidated earlier anti-discrimination statutes and lists religion or belief as a protected characteristic.
Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights protects manifestation of religion, subject to lawful and proportionate limits.
static.mainsAngle: Religious symbols in secular public institutions: how should democracies balance institutional neutrality with the right to manifest belief?

prelims: Articles 25–28 of the Indian Constitution deal with the right to freedom of religion; Article 25 covers all persons, Article 26 only religious denominations.
The 'essential religious practices' test, used to decide what religious practice attracts constitutional protection, originates in the Shirur Mutt case (1954).
The UK Equality Act 2010 lists 'religion or belief' as a protected characteristic, and Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights protects religious manifestation, subject to lawful limits.

Mounting extreme weather, land-use change and infrastructure pressure are compounding ecological stress. The report links the impasse to the gap between scientific recommendations and political-administrative follow-through.

static.topic: Western Ghats ecological protection and biodiversity conservation
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Biodiversity & Conservation
static.whatIsIt: The Western Ghats ecological protection zone refers to a proposed ecologically sensitive area (ESA) framework to regulate land use and development in the Western Ghats, a global biodiversity hotspot.
static.background: India is a megadiverse country; the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Biological Diversity Act 2002 and Forest Conservation Act 1980 form the legal core. The CBD (1992) and Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) set global conservation targets, including 30x30. Successive expert committees (Gadgil and Kasturirangan) recommended ecologically sensitive zones in the Western Ghats, but final notification has been repeatedly delayed.
static.geography: Western Ghats run parallel to India's western coast across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu; they influence monsoon patterns and harbour high endemism.
static.socioEconomic: The region supports agriculture, plantations, tourism, hydropower and dense human settlements; conservation rules affect livelihoods and development projects.
static.whyInNews: The proposed ecological protection zone notification remains stuck even as climate threats mount.
static.wayForward: Finalise a scientifically grounded ecologically sensitive zone framework with clear boundaries, participatory consultation, and balanced development safeguards.

static.topic: Climate change and India's commitments

static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle. Paris uses NDCs and a ratchet mechanism. Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and LiFE mission.
static.socioEconomic: Climate impacts such as extreme rainfall, landslides and heat stress affect vulnerable regions, including the Western Ghats.
static.whyInNews: Climate threats are cited as compounding the ecological risk in the Western Ghats while protection zone notification remains pending.
static.wayForward: Strengthen adaptation, disaster risk reduction and ecosystem-based resilience alongside mitigation commitments.
prelimsPointers: India's updated NDC: cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 by 2030.
Paris Agreement goal: keep warming well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C.

stories.headline: Supreme Court flags hurried elephant transfer from Assam to Tamil Nadu
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has raised concerns over the hurried transfer of elephants from Assam to Tamil Nadu, as reported by The News Minute. The intervention brings judicial scrutiny to an inter-state wildlife transfer that reportedly proceeded without adequate procedural care. The matter highlights questions of animal welfare, compliance with conservation norms, and coordination between state forest departments. stories.headline: Ten years after demonetisation, cash remains king in Indian payments
stories.summary: On 8 November 2016 the Union Government withdrew legal tender status from the ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes, citing black money, counterfeit currency and terror financing, and promising a decisive shift towards digital payments. Ten years on, reporting by The News Minute concludes that cash remains the dominant mode of payment in India, with currency in circulation continuing to expand even as UPI and other digital channels have grown rapidly. The outcome indicates that demonetisation reordered payment habits only partially, with digitisation concentrated among urban, smartphone-using and formally banked consumers, while small-value and informal transactions still run on cash. The anniversary has revived the debate over whether currency shocks are an effective instrument of economic policy and what a genuine formalisation strategy should look like.
stories.whyItMatters: It sits at the core of GS-III money and banking — currency management, the RBI's role, digital payments and formalisation of the economy — and connects to GS-II questions on financial inclusion and the real-world reach of governance interventions.

perspectives.take: Frames the ten-year anniversary around continuity rather than change — digitisation notwithstanding, cash is 'still king' in everyday Indian payments; a south-focused independent digital outlet, so the emphasis is on household and small-business payment behaviour.

static.topic: Demonetisation of 2016 and India's Currency Management Regime
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Money and Banking: currency, legal tender, RBI and monetary management
static.whatIsIt: Demonetisation was the withdrawal of legal tender status from the ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes announced on 8 November 2016, with new ₹500 and ₹2,000 notes issued in their place. It remains the most disruptive currency-management intervention in recent Indian economic history.
static.background: Announced on 8 November 2016 by the Union Government, the two highest denomination notes then in circulation ceased to be legal tender, with a limited window for deposit and exchange. The stated objectives were to curb black money, counterfeit currency and terror financing, and to accelerate a shift to digital payments. In 2023 the RBI announced the withdrawal of ₹2,000 banknotes from circulation, although they continue to be legal tender.
static.geography: Pan-India in scope. Cash dependence is generally higher in rural and semi-urban areas and in the informal economy, where digital connectivity, merchant infrastructure and banking access are uneven.
static.socioEconomic: The cash crunch fell hardest on informal-sector workers, small traders and daily-wage earners. The subsequent migration to UPI has been real but uneven, with benefits skewed towards those holding smartphones and formal bank accounts.
static.whyInNews: A decade after demonetisation, assessments indicate that cash continues to dominate Indian payments despite the rapid growth of digital transactions.
static.wayForward: Build digital and banking infrastructure in rural and informal segments, pursue anti-black-money enforcement through data and tax administration rather than currency shocks, and ensure an adequate, well-managed supply of currency while preserving the RBI's operational autonomy.
prelimsPointers: The RBI issues all banknotes from ₹2 upwards under Section 22 of the RBI Act, 1934; the ₹1 note and all coins are issued by the Government of India.

static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether demonetisation achieved its stated objectives, and examine whether currency management should be used as an instrument of broad economic policy.

static.topic: Digital Payments Ecosystem and Financial Inclusion

static.whatIsIt: India's retail digital payments stack — most prominently the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) — has grown into one of the largest retail payment systems in the world by transaction volume.
static.background: UPI was launched in 2016, the same year as demonetisation. It was enabled by the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) trinity, Aadhaar-based e-KYC, Digital India and a dense network of payment service providers. The RBI also launched pilots for a Central Bank Digital Currency (Digital Rupee) in 2022.
static.geography: Urban and semi-urban areas show high digital payment adoption; rural and remote regions lag in merchant acceptance infrastructure and connectivity.
static.socioEconomic: Digital payments lower transaction costs and improve traceability, but can exclude those without smartphones, reliable connectivity or formal accounts — which is part of why cash persists for small-value and informal transactions.
static.whyInNews: The ten-year anniversary of demonetisation has focused attention on why cash continues to dominate payments even as digital channels scale rapidly.
static.wayForward: Expand merchant acceptance and connectivity in underserved areas, strengthen consumer protection and grievance redressal, and treat digital payments and cash as complementary rather than mutually exclusive until inclusion gaps close.

stories.headline: China's factory-gate inflation hits near 4.5-year high as consumer prices stay muted
stories.summary: China's producer price index — which tracks factory-gate prices — rose in October at its fastest pace in nearly four-and-a-half years, according to official data reported on 9 November 2026. At the same time, consumer price inflation moderated, leaving retail price pressures subdued. The divergence points to cost-push pressure building at the producer level without a matching pickup in household demand. For trading partners, the signal matters because China is a dominant supplier of intermediate and capital goods, so its factory-gate prices feed into import costs across Asia and beyond.
stories.whyItMatters: Producer-versus-consumer price divergence in the world's second-largest economy shapes global tradable-goods inflation, commodity demand and the import-cost outlook for economies such as India. It is a live case study for UPSC on inflation measurement, monetary policy transmission and external-sector linkages.

perspectives.take: Data-led wire framing: factory-gate inflation at a multi-year high while the consumer price rise moderates — neutral, numbers-first reporting with no policy advocacy.
Hong Kong business daily stresses that producer-price momentum is building even as consumer price pressures stay muted — investor-facing, China-demand lens.
Malaysian market portal carries the same wire framing, underlining how Asian markets read Chinese price data for trade and commodity cues.

static.topic: Producer Price Index and the CPI–PPI Divergence
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Inflation and Price Indices
static.whatIsIt: A Producer Price Index (PPI) measures the average change in prices received by domestic producers for their output, capturing inflation at the factory gate before taxes and distribution margins. India does not yet publish a full-fledged PPI; the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) is used as a proxy for producer-level prices.
static.background: India's WPI has a base year of 2011-12 and is released monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, covering primary articles, fuel and power, and manufactured products. The Consumer Price Index (Combined) is compiled by the National Statistical Office under MoSPI with base year 2012, and food and beverages carry the largest weight in the basket. A technical working group has examined shifting India to a formal PPI framework.
static.socioEconomic: Producer-level price changes pass into retail prices with a lag, so a PPI spike can precede consumer inflation. In India, food and fuel dominate CPI volatility and directly affect household real incomes.
static.whyInNews: China's October producer prices rose at their fastest pace in nearly four-and-a-half years while consumer price growth moderated — a divergence that signals cost-push pressure at the factory gate without matching consumer demand.
static.wayForward: Move towards a formal PPI in India, strengthen pass-through analysis between producer and retail prices, and track imported inflation through WPI–CPI mapping.

static.mainsAngle: Discuss how producer-level price pressures transmit to retail inflation in India and what that implies for the timing and calibration of monetary policy.

static.topic: RBI, the Monetary Policy Committee and Inflation Targeting
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking and Monetary Policy
static.whatIsIt: The Reserve Bank of India, established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949 under the RBI Act, 1934, conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), instituted in 2016 with an inflation-targeting mandate of 4% CPI within a band of plus or minus 2%.
static.background: The MPC framework emerged from the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act. Policy tools include the repo and reverse repo rates, the Marginal Standing Facility, Cash Reserve Ratio, Statutory Liquidity Ratio and Open Market Operations. The RBI also regulates banks, manages forex reserves and acts as banker to the government.
static.socioEconomic: Inflation targeting anchors household inflation expectations and borrowing costs; the credibility of the framework shapes lending rates transmitted through MCLR and EBLR.
static.whyInNews: China's producer-versus-consumer price divergence illustrates the cost-push versus demand-pull dilemma central banks face; India's MPC operates a 4% CPI target with a 2–6% tolerance band.
static.wayForward: Balance growth support with price stability, improve transmission of rate decisions to borrowers, and strengthen fiscal-monetary coordination.
prelimsPointers: Repo is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
The MPC has six members — three from the RBI including the Governor as chair, and three external members; the Governor holds a casting vote.
The inflation target is 4% CPI with a 2–6% band, reviewed every five years.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how a central bank should respond when producer prices rise sharply but consumer demand remains weak, and assess the limits of inflation targeting in such a setting.

static.topic: China's Growth Model and India's Trade Exposure
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — External Sector and Global Linkages
static.whatIsIt: China is the world's second-largest economy and a dominant source of intermediate goods, capital goods and consumer imports for India. Its factory-gate prices therefore influence global tradable-goods prices and India's import bill.
static.background: China's accession to the WTO in 2001 cemented its role as the 'factory of the world'. Since the 2018 US-China trade tensions and the pandemic, 'China+1' supply-chain diversification has gained traction, with India's Production Linked Incentive schemes and Make in India aimed at capturing part of that shift. India's trade deficit with China remains among its largest.
static.geography: East Asia; China shares land borders with 14 countries, and India-China trade moves largely by sea as well as through border trade points such as Nathu La.
static.socioEconomic: Chinese demand conditions affect commodity exporters globally. Cheaper Chinese goods can pressure Indian micro, small and medium enterprises, while costlier Chinese inputs raise production costs for Indian manufacturers.
static.whyInNews: Rising Chinese factory-gate inflation could raise input costs for Indian importers and shift the terms of trade for Asian manufacturing economies.
static.wayForward: Diversify import sources, deepen domestic manufacturing capability, monitor dumping risks and strengthen trade remedy mechanisms.
prelimsPointers: China is among India's largest trading partners and a major contributor to India's trade deficit.
Anti-dumping and countervailing investigations in India are conducted by the Directorate General of Trade Remedies under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how shifts in China's price and growth dynamics transmit to India's inflation, trade balance and manufacturing competitiveness.

stories.headline: Trump signals likely Xi, Putin meetings at China-hosted APEC summit
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has said he expects to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the margins of the APEC summit being hosted by China. The remarks, carried by multiple outlets, point to the possibility of high-level face-to-face diplomacy involving three of the world's major nuclear-armed powers at a single venue. Neither Beijing nor Moscow has publicly confirmed any such meetings, and no schedule has been verified. The statement lands amid continuing US-China trade and technology friction and the unresolved war in Ukraine, both of which would shape any agenda. The episode also highlights how China's role as APEC host is being read as a marker of its diplomatic centrality in the Asia-Pacific.
stories.whyItMatters: APEC is a recurring venue for great-power bilateralism, so the story feeds directly into GS-II questions on summit diplomacy, US-China-Russia triangularity and India's positioning between blocs.

perspectives.take: Wire-service framing: attributes the claim squarely to Trump, keeps to reported statements and avoids confirming any meeting — global, agency-style neutrality.

static.topic: Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC)
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Regional Groupings & Fora
static.whatIsIt: A voluntary, consensus-based economic forum of 21 Asia-Pacific economies created to promote trade and investment liberalisation and broader economic cooperation across the Pacific rim. It is not a treaty-based organisation and its commitments are non-binding.
static.background: APEC began in 1989 in Canberra as an informal ministerial dialogue among twelve economies and expanded through the 1990s to take in China, Hong Kong, Chinese Taipei, Mexico, Papua New Guinea, Chile, Peru, Russia and Vietnam. The 1994 Bogor Goals set targets for free and open trade; the 2020 Putrajaya Vision 2040 replaced them with a longer-horizon agenda. A moratorium on admitting new members has been in place since 1997.
static.geography: Asia-Pacific rim — East Asia, Southeast Asia, Oceania, the Pacific coast of the Americas and Russia's Far East; the Secretariat is located in Singapore.
static.socioEconomic: APEC economies together account for roughly three-fifths of world GDP and close to half of global trade. Its agenda spans trade facilitation, structural reform, the digital economy and, increasingly, climate and food security.
static.whyInNews: China is hosting APEC 2026, and US President Donald Trump has said he expects to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin there.
static.wayForward: India is not a member, so its practical channels into Asia-Pacific economic governance remain the East Asia Summit, the Indo-Pacific frameworks and bilateral trade negotiations; APEC nonetheless serves as a benchmark for regional trade architecture.
prelimsPointers: APEC was founded in 1989 and has 21 member economies; India is not a member.
APEC decisions are non-binding and taken by consensus; its Secretariat is in Singapore.
China is the host economy for APEC 2026.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how APEC's non-binding, consensus-based model compares with treaty-based groupings such as RCEP and CPTPP, and what that implies for India's trade strategy in the Indo-Pacific.

static.topic: Great-Power Summitry: US–China–Russia Dynamics
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bipolarity, Multipolarity & India's Strategic Autonomy
static.whatIsIt: The practice of major-power leaders using multilateral summits as venues for bilateral or trilateral diplomacy — to manage crises, set negotiating frameworks or signal intent without entering formal commitments.
static.background: Summit-level diplomacy shaped the Cold War (Geneva 1955, Reykjavik 1986) and the post-Cold War order, and has more recently been used to try to manage the war in Ukraine and the US-China trade and technology rivalry. Multilateral venues — G20, APEC, BRICS, SCO — have repeatedly served as cover for bilateral meetings on the sidelines.
static.socioEconomic: US-China tariff measures and export controls, together with sanctions on Russia, have reshaped supply chains, energy flows and technology standards, with direct consequences for Indian industry, trade and energy sourcing.
static.whyInNews: Trump's stated expectation of meeting Xi and Putin at APEC 2026 raises the prospect of simultaneous high-level US engagement with both rivals at one venue.
static.wayForward: India's interest lies in preserving strategic autonomy, avoiding absorption into bloc confrontation, and using its own summit platforms to keep supply chains, energy access and defence partnerships diversified.
prelimsPointers: APEC, G20, BRICS and SCO are among the principal multilateral venues used for leader-level bilateral meetings.
India is a member of the G20, BRICS, SCO and the East Asia Summit, but not of APEC.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how simultaneous great-power engagement at multilateral summits affects the room for manoeuvre available to middle powers such as India.

stories.headline: Karnataka High Court: Enforcement Directorate is not a 'super cop'
stories.summary: The Karnataka High Court, while dealing with a matter involving the Enforcement Directorate, observed that the agency is not a 'super cop' and must act strictly within the boundaries drawn by statute. The remark is the latest judicial signal that statutory investigative agencies cannot assume powers beyond those Parliament has conferred, and that courts will examine arrests, attachments and summons for procedural compliance. It lands amid a continuing national debate over the ED's use of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act — its power to attach proceeds of crime, summon accused persons and make arrests — provisions whose constitutional validity the Supreme Court upheld in 2022 while underlining safeguards. The observation also reaffirms the High Court's Article 226 role in reviewing the conduct of executive and statutory authorities.
stories.whyItMatters: It goes to the constitutional limits of statutory investigative agencies and the extent of judicial review over arrest, attachment and summons powers — a recurring GS-II theme on checks and balances, federalism and personal liberty.

perspectives.take: Frames the ruling as a judicial rebuke to the ED's self-image of untrammelled authority, foregrounding civil-liberties and accountability concerns; the outlet's editorial line is generally critical of central agencies' use against political opponents.
