static.topic: Enforcement Directorate and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Statutory and regulatory bodies; role of investigative agencies
static.whatIsIt: The Enforcement Directorate is a multi-disciplinary investigative agency under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance. It enforces the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA), the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 and the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974 (COFEPOSA).
static.background: An 'Enforcement Unit' was set up in 1956 in the Department of Economic Affairs to investigate violations of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act; it was renamed the Enforcement Directorate in 1957 and moved to the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance, in 1960. The PMLA was enacted in 2002 and came into force in 2005, creating the offence of money laundering, the power to attach proceeds of crime, and Special Courts. The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act followed in 2018. In Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (2022), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of key PMLA provisions, including those on arrest, attachment and the reverse burden of proof, while emphasising procedural safeguards; later rulings have continued to test the manner in which arrest and summons powers are exercised.
static.socioEconomic: Coercive action by the agency affects business confidence, the credit and investment climate, and the liberty of persons accused before trial, making procedural fairness economically and socially significant.
static.whyInNews: The Karnataka High Court's remark that the ED is not a 'super cop' has renewed scrutiny of the agency's arrest, attachment and summons powers under the PMLA.
static.wayForward: Codify clearer thresholds for arrest and attachment, ensure reasoned and recorded satisfaction before coercive steps, strengthen the adjudication and appellate chain, and reinforce internal accountability and oversight.

The PMLA was enacted in 2002 and came into force in 2005; it created the offence of money laundering and the power to attach proceeds of crime.
The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act was enacted in 2018.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether the coercive powers of investigative agencies such as the ED are adequately balanced by procedural safeguards and judicial oversight.

stories.headline: Deepavali fires kill six in MP; blazes in Mumbai, Hyderabad
stories.summary: A string of fire accidents around Deepavali left casualties and stretched fire services across three States. In Mumbai, a major blaze broke out in the Dongri area, with the Fire Brigade declaring a Level-I call at 10.11 p.m. and deploying its personnel alongside police, BEST, ward staff and the 108 ambulance service; a separate high-rise fire on November 7 had already claimed one life. In Hyderabad, firecracker shops and godowns saw repeated incidents, including a blaze at a plastic manufacturing unit in Katedan Industrial Area that spread to an adjoining plywood unit and required three fire engines. In Madhya Pradesh, six members of a family were killed when a fire engulfed a three-storey building housing a crockery shop in Barhi town, Katni district, around midnight. Together the incidents point to recurring gaps in fire-safety compliance in dense commercial and residential premises rather than a single cause.
stories.whyItMatters: Fire safety sits at the intersection of urban governance, building regulation and disaster management — a recurring GS-III disaster-management theme with GS-II governance and federalism angles. The Deepavali cluster is a ready case study on enforcement failure and on whether fire services should remain a purely State subject.

perspectives.take: Mumbai city-desk report foregrounds the municipal response machinery — the Level-I call and multi-agency deployment — framing the Dongri blaze as an urban fire-response and preparedness story.
Hyderabad edition ties the Deepavali spike to unregulated firecracker shops and godowns, framing it as a licensing, storage and industrial-safety failure rather than an accident.

static.topic: Fire safety in urban India: regulation and enforcement
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — urban and industrial fire hazards; government policies and regulation
static.whatIsIt: Fire services are a State subject under Entry 12 of the State List (Seventh Schedule), so fire stations, equipment and enforcement are run by State governments and municipal corporations. Technical standards come from the National Building Code of India (Bureau of Indian Standards), whose Part 4 deals with fire and life safety, and from State and municipal building bye-laws largely modelled on the Model Building Bye-laws issued by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. A Fire No-Conversion Certificate (fire NOC) from the local fire authority is a precondition for occupancy of specified building categories.
static.background: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) moved 'disaster management' to the Concurrent List (Entry 23), but fire services were left in the State List. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 — enacted after the 1999 Odisha super-cyclone, the 2001 Bhuj earthquake and the 2004 tsunami — created the NDMA, SDMAs and DDMAs and the NDRF, but its focus is largely on natural hazards. Repeated fire tragedies in high-rise buildings, hospitals, coaching centres and commercial complexes have led courts to order fire-safety audits and closure of non-compliant premises. There have been proposals to shift fire services to the Concurrent List so that a central law and uniform standards can apply.
static.geography: High-density, mixed-use urban cores with narrow lanes and encroached access routes — old city areas such as Dongri in Mumbai — often prevent fire tenders from reaching the seat of a fire in time.
static.socioEconomic: Small workshops, godowns and family-run shops in dense neighbourhoods frequently operate without fire NOCs, adequate exits or stored-water arrangements; compliance costs are seen as unaffordable for informal enterprises, and enforcement is thin.
static.whyInNews: Fires in Mumbai's Dongri, at firecracker shops and godowns in Hyderabad, and at a crockery shop in Katni (Madhya Pradesh) around Deepavali killed at least six people and required large multi-agency deployments.
static.wayForward: Link fire NOCs to trade licences and property tax records so that non-compliance has commercial consequences; mandate periodic third-party fire audits with public disclosure; enforce hydrant, exit and access-lane standards in bye-laws; modernise State fire services with central assistance; and include fire-safety drills in school and hospital accreditation.
keyTerms: National Building Code of India, Part 4
prelimsPointers: 'Fire services' is Entry 12 of the State List; 'disaster management' is Entry 23 of the Concurrent List, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
The National Building Code of India is published by the Bureau of Indian Standards; its Part 4 covers fire and life safety.
Model Building Bye-laws are issued by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and adopted with modifications by States and municipal bodies.
static.mainsAngle: Recurring urban fires show that the binding constraint is enforcement, not the absence of standards. Examine why fire-safety norms fail at the municipal level and evaluate the case for moving fire services to the Concurrent List.

static.topic: India's disaster management architecture
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — institutional framework and mandate
static.whatIsIt: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 provides the statutory architecture: the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) chaired by the Prime Minister, State Disaster Management Authorities chaired by Chief Ministers, District Disaster Management Authorities chaired by District Magistrates, and the National Disaster Response Force as the specialised response arm. The National Policy on Disaster Management and the National Disaster Management Plan set out prevention, mitigation, preparedness and response priorities.
static.background: The Act followed a decade of major disasters — the 1999 Odisha super-cyclone, the 2001 Bhuj earthquake and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami — and the recommendations of the High Powered Committee on Disaster Management. India is a signatory to the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030), which shifted global emphasis from relief to risk reduction. Fire and industrial accidents fall within the 'man-made disaster' category, but primary response capacity rests with State fire services rather than the NDRF.
static.socioEconomic: Rapid, often unplanned urbanisation concentrates population and economic assets in hazard-prone, poorly serviced built environments, raising the risk of man-made disasters such as fires and structural collapses.
static.whyInNews: The Deepavali-period fires in Mumbai, Hyderabad and Katni illustrate how man-made fire hazards are handled largely by State and municipal agencies, with the national disaster framework playing a supporting role.
static.wayForward: Strengthen district-level risk assessment and fire-hazard mapping; integrate fire risk into city disaster management plans; build State fire services' capacity with central financial assistance; and treat fire as a distinct hazard with dedicated mitigation funding.
prelimsPointers: The NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister; SDMAs by Chief Ministers and DDMAs by District Magistrates.
The NDRF was raised in 2006 as a specialised response force under the Disaster Management Act, 2005.
The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030) succeeded the Hyogo Framework and emphasises risk reduction over relief.
static.mainsAngle: India's disaster management framework is oriented towards natural hazards. Discuss whether man-made hazards such as urban fires need a distinct institutional and funding response.

static.topic: Regulation of firecrackers: manufacture, storage and use
static.syllabusNode: Environment and disaster management — hazardous substances regulation; role of regulatory bodies
static.whatIsIt: The manufacture, storage, transport and sale of firecrackers are regulated under the Explosives Act, 1884, the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 and the Petroleum Act, 1934, with licences issued by the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), which functions under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade. Municipal and police licensing governs retail sale, and the Supreme Court has issued a series of directions on the composition and timing of firecracker bursting.
static.background: Judicial intervention on firecrackers has centred on air pollution, particularly in the National Capital Region, with orders restricting the sale and use of certain categories of crackers and limiting bursting to specified hours. The concept of 'green crackers' — reduced-emission formulations developed with CSIR-NEERI — emerged from this litigation. Storage of crackers in residential and commercial godowns without licence remains a persistent safety hazard.
static.geography: Firecracker manufacturing is concentrated in a few clusters, notably in Tamil Nadu, while storage and retail godowns are distributed across cities, often in densely built neighbourhoods.
static.socioEconomic: The firecracker industry supports large-scale direct and indirect employment, so restrictions carry livelihood implications; at the same time, unlicensed godowns in residential areas expose workers and neighbours to severe risk.
static.whyInNews: A series of fire incidents at firecracker shops and godowns in Hyderabad marred Deepavali, highlighting storage-safety and licensing failures.
static.wayForward: Enforce licensed-only storage away from residential clusters; conduct pre-festival inspections of retail outlets and godowns; promote green crackers through standards and incentives; and run public awareness on safe bursting practices.
prelimsPointers: PESO, the licensing authority for explosives and petroleum, functions under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade.
'Green crackers' are reduced-emission formulations developed with CSIR-NEERI following Supreme Court directions on firecracker use.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing livelihood dependence on the firecracker industry with air-quality and fire-safety concerns requires a regulatory rather than a prohibitory approach. Critically examine.

prelims: 'Fire services' is a State subject (Entry 12, State List); 'disaster management' is a Concurrent List subject (Entry 23) after the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

The National Building Code of India, published by the Bureau of Indian Standards, deals with fire and life safety in Part 4; Model Building Bye-laws are issued by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs.
The NDMA under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 is chaired by the Prime Minister, and the NDRF is its specialised response force.

stories.mainsQuestion: Urban fire accidents recur in Indian cities despite a well-developed set of building and fire-safety standards. Examine the reasons for weak enforcement at the municipal level and evaluate the case for moving fire services from the State List to the Concurrent List.

stories.headline: Samvat 2083 opens tepid as Nifty slips below 25,000; rupee, bonds hold firm
stories.summary: The first trading session of Samvat 2083 was muted, with the Sensex shedding roughly 100 points to close around 80,886.75 and the Nifty slipping below the 25,000 mark as IT and power counters dragged. Sectoral divergence was sharp: banks and pharma held firm, with SBI emerging as the top Nifty gainer, up about 1.82%, while smaller companies and select mid-cap names advanced. In the Muhurat session a day earlier, 14 NSE 500 stocks — including ICICI Bank and Divi's Laboratories — touched new highs, and Tata Steel gained about 3% after steady Q2 earnings. Participation is expected to stay low through the festive week, with the market closed on Tuesday. In parallel, the rupee was expected to open in the 93.92–93.98 band after settling at 93.9050 to the dollar on Friday, while bond traders remained constructive on the back of benign crude oil prices and softer US Treasury yields.
stories.whyItMatters: Festive-season sessions are a useful entry point to revise capital market structure, index mechanics and the rupee/bond transmission channels — all recurring GS-III themes on market regulation, external sector stability and monetary policy transmission.

perspectives.take: Frames the session as a narrow, low-conviction market: index-level weakness from IT and power stocks, offset by bank and pharma strength, with bond bulls and rupee traders guided by global cues rather than domestic festive sentiment.

Emphasises the breadth story beneath the flat headline — smaller companies gaining and specific NSE 500 scrips and Tata Steel hitting new highs — treating the Muhurat session as one of selective stock-specific action rather than a broad trend.

static.topic: Muhurat Trading, the Samvat Calendar and Indian Equity Indices
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Capital Markets and Financial Market Structure
static.whatIsIt: Muhurat trading is a customary special one-hour trading session conducted by the BSE and NSE on Diwali/Lakshmi Puja, marking the ceremonial beginning of the new accounting year in the Vikram Samvat calendar. It is a symbolic session in which trades are executed, settled and carry the same legal force as any other trading day.
static.background: Vikram Samvat is a Hindu calendar era traditionally associated with King Vikramaditya; the new Samvat year begins around Diwali. Indian exchanges have held Muhurat trading for decades, and both BSE and NSE now conduct it simultaneously in a single-hour evening window timed to Lakshmi Puja. The BSE Sensex (S&P BSE Sensex) is a 30-stock index launched in 1986 with base year 1978-79 and base value 100; the NSE's Nifty 50 is a 50-stock index launched in 1996 with base year 1995 and base value 1000. Index construction, free-float weighting and surveillance are regulated by SEBI, which was set up in 1988 and given statutory powers under the SEBI Act, 1992.
static.socioEconomic: Muhurat trading blends a cultural/religious observance with financial-market ritual, and is closely watched as a sentiment indicator for household and retail participation. Its market impact is largely psychological — turnover is thin and not representative of underlying liquidity.
static.whyInNews: Samvat 2083 commenced on 8 November 2026 with a tepid first session: the Sensex and Nifty slipped, even as smaller companies, select NSE 500 scrips and Tata Steel bucked the trend.
static.wayForward: For exam purposes, treat Muhurat sessions as market-structure and investor-sentiment illustrations rather than as economic signals. Regulators and exchanges could use the visibility of such sessions to push investor education, given the sharp rise in retail and first-time investor participation.
prelimsPointers: Sensex: 30 scrips, base year 1978-79, base value 100, launched in 1986; Nifty 50: base year 1995, base value 1000, launched in 1996.
Muhurat trading is a special one-hour session held on Diwali/Lakshmi Puja to mark the start of the new Samvat year.
SEBI was constituted in 1988 and obtained statutory powers through the SEBI Act, 1992; its headquarters is in Mumbai.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how cultural and behavioural factors such as festive sentiment interact with market fundamentals, and assess whether rising retail participation in Indian equity markets warrants stronger investor-protection safeguards.

static.topic: Rupee Exchange Rate and India's Managed Float
static.syllabusNode: Economy — External Sector and Foreign Exchange Management
static.whatIsIt: The external value of the rupee is determined largely by market forces under a managed floating regime, in which the Reserve Bank of India intervenes in the spot and forward markets to curb excessive volatility rather than to target a specific level. The FBIL reference rate serves as the daily benchmark.
static.background: India moved away from a fixed peg through the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) of 1992, followed by the unification of the dual exchange rate in 1993, effectively shifting to a market-determined rate. The rupee remains only partially convertible on the capital account. India's foreign exchange reserves — held mainly as foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position with the IMF — are the primary buffer used for intervention and for import cover.
static.socioEconomic: A weaker rupee raises imported inflation (notably crude oil and edible oil) and the cost of overseas education and travel, while aiding exporters such as IT services and textiles. Exchange-rate movements therefore redistribute gains and losses across households and firms.
static.whyInNews: Traders expected the rupee to open in the 93.92–93.98 band on 9 November 2026, after it settled at 93.9050 to the dollar on Friday, with the recent rally facing a test as global market jitters linked to AI-related stocks eased.
static.wayForward: Sustaining rupee stability depends on a contained current account deficit, healthy capital inflows, predictable RBI communication and diversification of export markets and the external funding mix.
prelimsPointers: India follows a managed floating exchange rate regime; the rupee is not fully convertible on the capital account.
FBIL publishes the daily rupee reference rate; the RBI intervenes mainly through the spot and forward markets.
Foreign exchange reserves comprise foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position with the IMF.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the trade-offs the RBI faces in managing exchange-rate volatility when global risk sentiment shifts sharply, and evaluate the implications of a weak rupee for inflation, the current account and export competitiveness.

static.topic: Government Securities Market and Bond Yields
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Financial Markets, Monetary Policy Transmission and Public Debt
static.whatIsIt: The government securities (G-sec) market is where the Union and State governments raise market borrowings through auctions conducted by the RBI, and where the benchmark yields that price nearly all other debt in the economy are discovered. Bond prices and yields move inversely.
static.background: The RBI conducts primary auctions of dated G-secs and Treasury bills and manages the market borrowing calendar along with the Union government. State Development Loans (SDLs) are issued on behalf of states. Deregulation of interest rates, introduction of electronic trading platforms and phased FPI investment limits in G-secs deepened the market over the 1990s and 2000s. India's phased inclusion in major global emerging-market bond indices — JPMorgan's GBI-EM Global Diversified from June 2024, Bloomberg's EM local currency index from January 2025 and FTSE Russell's EM government bond index from September 2025 — has improved the prospect of steady passive inflows.
static.socioEconomic: Bond yields act as the risk-free benchmark for household borrowing costs — home, auto and MSME loans — and also determine the government's interest outgo, which competes with capital and welfare expenditure in the budget.
static.whyInNews: Fundamentals were seen as favouring bond bulls on 9 November 2026, with benign crude oil prices and softer US Treasury yields improving investor sentiment and raising the prospect of further gains in Indian bonds.
static.wayForward: Deepening the corporate bond market, widening the investor base beyond banks and mutual funds, and maintaining fiscal credibility through a credible consolidation path would help anchor yields and lower the cost of public borrowing.
prelimsPointers: Bond price and yield are inversely related; a fall in yield signals a rise in bond prices.
The RBI auctions Central and State government securities and manages the borrowing calendar.
India began phased inclusion in global emerging-market bond indices from 2024, which can support passive foreign inflows.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate how global monetary conditions and commodity prices transmit to India's sovereign bond market, and discuss whether deeper foreign participation in G-secs enhances or complicates domestic macroeconomic stability.

stories.headline: Asian markets steady as AI, West Asia worries ease; gold gains on softer oil
stories.summary: Asian equity markets held broadly steady as two overhangs — anxiety over stretched AI-linked valuations and West Asia geopolitical risk — began to unwind, while the dollar stayed firm on expectations about the US Federal Reserve's rate path. Gold rose more than 1%, helped by softer crude prices that reduced inflation worries and revived demand for the metal as a hedge. A pullback in AI-themed stocks has pushed investors to rotate back into Asia's long-neglected, under-owned 'old economy' trades. For India, the combination matters through three channels: imported inflation via crude, the rupee's level against a firm dollar, and foreign portfolio flows that respond to US rate expectations.
stories.whyItMatters: Global risk sentiment, US monetary policy and crude prices transmit directly into India's inflation, currency and capital flows — the exact variables the MPC weighs while setting the repo rate. This is a live GS-III economy question with a GS-II international-linkage angle.

perspectives.take: Frames the session as risk-on stabilisation — Asian equities steady, dollar firm on Fed rate bets, with AI and Middle East risk premia unwinding; wire-service, market-move focused.
Reads the commodities channel: softer oil eases inflation fears, lifting gold over 1% — a signal on real rates and safe-haven demand rather than on growth.
Turns the AI selloff into a rotation story — capital returning to Asia's forgotten value and old-economy trades; India-centric business daily, investor-flow lens.

static.topic: Reserve Bank of India & Monetary Policy
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy
static.whatIsIt: India's central bank, established in 1935 (nationalised 1949) under the RBI Act, 1934. It conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), instituted in 2016 with an inflation-targeting mandate of 4% CPI (±2%).
static.background: The MPC framework came from the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act. Policy tools include repo/reverse repo, the Marginal Standing Facility, Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) and Open Market Operations. The RBI also regulates banks, manages forex reserves and acts as banker to the government.
static.socioEconomic: Rate decisions transmit to households and firms through MCLR/EBLR-linked loans, affecting EMIs, MSME credit costs and savers' deposit returns; external shocks such as a firm dollar or costlier crude complicate the growth-inflation trade-off.
static.whyInNews: A firm dollar driven by US Fed rate expectations shapes the interest-rate differential, FPI flows and the rupee, all of which feed into the RBI's inflation and liquidity calculus.
static.wayForward: Strengthen monetary transmission, maintain an adequate forex buffer, and coordinate fiscal and monetary policy so that external shocks do not de-anchor inflation expectations.
prelimsPointers: Repo is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
The MPC has six members — three from the RBI (Governor as chair) and three external; the Governor holds a casting vote.
Inflation target: 4% CPI with a 2–6% band, reviewed every five years.
static.mainsAngle: Balance growth support with price stability; examine transmission of rate changes to borrowers via MCLR/EBLR and the role of fiscal-monetary coordination.

static.topic: Crude oil prices and India's external sector
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Inflation, Energy Security & External Sector
static.whatIsIt: India meets a large majority of its crude oil requirement through imports, so Brent price movements pass into the import bill, the current account deficit, the rupee and domestic inflation.
static.background: India's oil import dependence rose sharply after the 1990s liberalisation and has been a recurring macro vulnerability during every global oil spike. Policy responses have included phased fuel-price deregulation, ethanol blending, expansion of strategic petroleum reserves and a push on renewables and electric mobility.
static.geography: West Asia supply routes matter directly — the Strait of Hormuz carries a large share of seaborne crude destined for Asia, so any disruption there is transmitted straight into Asian import prices.
static.socioEconomic: Costlier fuel feeds into transport, food and administered prices, squeezing household budgets; softer crude eases the import bill, subsidy pressure and the current account.
static.whyInNews: Softer oil prices were cited as easing inflation worries and lifting gold by more than 1% in the 9 November 2026 Reuters report.
static.wayForward: Diversify crude sourcing, expand strategic petroleum reserves, and accelerate ethanol blending, renewables and electrification to structurally reduce import dependence.
prelimsPointers: Crude oil influences both CPI (through fuel and transport) and WPI.
A stronger dollar makes India's imports costlier and can trigger foreign portfolio outflows.
Gold is a safe-haven asset; its price typically moves inversely with real interest rates and the dollar.
static.mainsAngle: Link external-sector shocks to domestic inflation management and energy security, and evaluate how far India can insulate itself.

prelims: Gold is a safe-haven asset: prices typically rise when real yields fall, the dollar softens or risk aversion increases.
A firm dollar, driven by US Fed rate expectations, raises India's import costs and can pull foreign portfolio capital out of emerging markets.
Crude oil is a key input into India's import bill and feeds into both CPI and WPI, making softer oil disinflationary for importers.
The RBI's MPC targets 4% CPI inflation within a 2–6% band — external price shocks are central to its rate decisions.
stories.mainsQuestion: Examine how global risk sentiment, US monetary policy and crude oil prices transmit into India's inflation, exchange rate and capital flows. How effectively can domestic monetary policy insulate the economy from such external shocks?
